#309. NVIDIA shareholders are suing the company and CEO Jensen Huang

The company’s shares have plummeted in response to the exec’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The unfolding drama around NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman now accused of being a spy for the Chinese government may be getting its first courtroom chapter. A shareholder in the computing giant has sued accusing NVIDIA and Huang of misleading investors about the nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Taiwanese company Megaspeed who is now suspected of being an espionage asset for China. Huang is a common surname; The pair are not related.

Mark Kistenmacher filed the complaint and is seeking class action status for anyone who purchased NVIDIA shares between October 9 and November 8. The first date is when The New York Times published a story on NVIDIA and Megaspeed detailing a connection between the pair, which was rebuffed by NVIDIA as a routine business relationship; the second date is when the NVIDIA founder admitted to an affair and the company publicly disclosed that it was launching its own investigation into whether its top exec had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

In the interim, The New York Times published an in-depth feature on October 29 claiming that the NVIDIA CEO had become the subject of a suspected Chinese intelligence action. The piece cites NVIDIA representative John Rizzo, who said, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." This statement, the lawsuit alleges, was not true.

The company's shares have dropped in the fallout of the allegations, with NVIDIA on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over the past two days. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint states.

#308. Steam Deck performance gets a reality check with Valve's new FPS data

Benchmark tools for generic gaming rigs could be coming soon.

Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021, players have found that a game’s “Verified” status doesn’t always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games.

Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February. Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED.

Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don’t account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. Regardless, Valve says it has nonetheless “found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges.”

This kind of data can be extremely useful for distinguishing between the wide range of performance levels that can exist among “Verified” Steam Deck games. Both Cyberpunk 2077 and Skyrim: Special Edition earn the same Steam Deck Verified badge, for instance, but the former sees average Deck frame rates in the 30–40 FPS range, while the latter usually achieves 50–60 FPS on the hardware.

Valve’s frame rate data is even more useful for games that the company insists are “Unsupported” on Steam Deck because their “graphics setting cannot be configured to run well” on the hardware or because Valve is “still working on adding support for this game.” Despite warnings like these, games like Starfield, Silent Hill 2, and Assassin’s Creed Syndicate, to name just a few, all show extremely playable frame rates reported by actual Steam Deck users. Assassin’s Creed Syndicate in particular approaches a 60 FPS average on the Steam Deck OLED hardware despite its “Unsupported” status.

Frame rate data can also be useful for judging the single-player modes of games whose multiplayer doesn’t work under SteamOS. Watch Dogs 2, for example, is officially Unsupported on Steam Deck because of anti-cheat compatibility issues, but Steam Deck players report averages of 40+ FPS on the game’s single-player modes.

Of course, collecting and averaging frame rate data for the Steam Deck(s) is made simpler by their set hardware configuration. When it comes to communicating expected frame rates for the wide range of hardware in more generalized gaming PCs, Valve says it is “always looking for new ways to help developers understand the experiences customers are having with their games.”

Back in April, JSON files buried in the Steam client pointed to a potential Steam “Framerate Estimator” tool that could let users “Select an App and a PC config to get a chart of estimated framerates, based on the framerates of other Steam users,” according to strings contained within. That could be incredibly useful for Steam users who want to go beyond the listed Minimum and Recommended hardware requirements without relying on shady-looking third-party FPS-estimator websites. In the meantime, is sharing average frame rate data for the fixed-configuration Steam Machine too much to ask?

#306. How to get this Siri camera upgrade for your iPad before its public release

You’ll be able to access Visual Intelligence from a new tab in the tablet's Camera app.

Apple users willing to install beta versions of its OS updates can get their hands on upcoming features sooner than most, as long as they're comfortable contending with the possibility of buggy software or apps breaking. And one such feature is the Siri Mode that's already available in the camera app on supported iPhones. It's also coming to compatible iPads as part of iPadOS 27.3 and will let you ask Siri AI questions about things you point your tablet's camera at.

We got our first look at this mode when Apple properly unveiled Siri AI at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June this year. It basically brings the company's Visual Intelligence tool for asking questions from photos to the camera app. But there's one distinguishing feature that's unique to iPads which isn't available on iPhones.

On iPads, Visual Intelligence includes Apple Pencil support. So, much like with Google's Circle to Search feature, you can snap a photo of something with your iPad, use your Apple Pencil to draw a circle around an item and learn more information about the object with the help of Siri AI.

It's worth noting that Visual Intelligence is already available on compatible tablets — iPad Pro and iPad Air with the M1 chip and newer, and iPad mini with the A17 Pro or A20 Pro chipset. As things stand, you can access it in the Camera app by long-pressing the Camera Control button or pressing the Action button if you've set it up to activate the feature (and your iPad has an Action button, of course).

In iPadOS 27.3, you'll have another way to access Visual Intelligence in the Camera app. All you'll have to do is swipe through the options in the viewfinder (i.e. photo, video and portrait modes) until you get to the Siri tab.

The company is expected to release the public version of iPadOS 27.3 in December. However, you can try it on your tablet right now, because Apple released the first beta in early November.

To install the iPadOS 27.3 beta, open the Settings app on your iPad, then tap General > Software Update. If you haven't already done so, you'll need to enable beta updates. Tap the Beta Updates option, then iPadOS 27 Public Beta. After you go back to the Software Update tab, you should be able to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta.

Before you install the beta, it's best to create a full backup of your iPad using iCloud, a Mac or a Windows PC. Beta builds aren't the finished product, meaning they're more susceptible to bugs and errors. Backing up your data should be standard practice anyway, but it's especially advisable to do that before installing a beta version of an operating system, just to make sure your files and other information stay safe.

If you don't feel comfortable enough to install a iPadOS beta, that's perfectly fine! The public version of the OS update is likely coming soon. You can check out the Siri tab on your iPad's Camera app at that point.

#305. Krakow mass shooting suspect has died in hospital, police in Poland say

The alleged gunman who killed six people in a shooting spree in the Polish city of Krakow has died of injuries sustained in a shootout with police, authorities say.

The alleged shooter who went on a shooting rampage in the Polish city of Krakow on Saturday has died two days after being critically wounded by officers, police said on Monday.

"We inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died this morning in the hospital," regional police said in a post on X.

The man drove past the square in Krakow's Old Town, an area of Poland's second-largest city visited by many tourists, and carried out the shooting. He continued shooting even after suffering wounds by police officers, according to the authorities.

He is also suspected of killing his parents and sister at his family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles), before carrying out the alleged attack in central Krakow.

Six people were killed and 15 wounded in the shooting spree by the 24-year-old Polish man who allegedly carried out the attack.

The victims were of various nationalities. Three women and one man were Polish, with two other victims being an Austrian woman and a British man. The list of people injured includes people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The two officers who stopped the assailant also remained in hospital.

The shooting is being investigated as a terrorist offense. While Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the assailant held radical and ultranationalist views, no information has been given as to whether he was a member of any extremist organization.

Grief and shock took over Poland after the shooting.

The attack's site at the city's central square became a place of commemoration as many people laid candles and flowers.

The St. Mary's Trumpet Call, the melody played at Krakow's Main Square every hour, stopped in honor of the victims.  This was the first time this happened since World War II. The St. Anne's Church received a wave of mourners who came to attend a service for the victims.

Mass shootings are not common in Poland. Some 411,000 hold gun permits across the country, with interest in gun ownership being on the rise.

#304. Free video-streaming service Tubi lets users share curated watchlists now

User-based recommendations could make it easier to find stuff to watch on Tubi.

Tubi users can now create and share playlists of movies and shows available on the streaming service.

Tubi is a free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) service that has both live channels and on-demand content.

Today, the Fox-owned company announced “Mixtapes” as a way for users to make watchlists from Tubi’s “nearly 400,000 movies and TV episodes,” Tubi’s announcement said, adding:

They can give each mixtape a title and description and arrange the entertainment inside in whatever order feels right to them. Viewers can build one entirely on their own, or describe what they’re looking for and let Tubi offer a starting place that they can edit, rearrange, or rebuild entirely. When their mixtape is finished, they can publish and share it with other people or keep it for themselves.

Tubi’s Mixtapes website already features numerous playlists, including: “Millennial Memory Lane”—with movies like Cruel Intentions (1999) and The Fifth Element (1997) and shows such as Everybody Hates Chris (2005–2009) and Degrassi: The Next Generation (2001–2015); and “Bald Baddies”—which includes Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw (2019) and Central Intelligence (2016).

Watching a Mixtape doesn’t require a Tubi account, but making one does.

Tubi’s Mixtapes comes at a time when streaming service providers are seeking a way to address the content fragmentation that’s frequently cited as a frustration among streaming users, as well as users struggling to find something to watch. Gracenote’s “2025 State of Play” report, for instance, surveyed 3,000 consumers in the US, Brazil, France, Germany, Mexico, and the UK and found that “nearly 33 percent of streaming users feel content and service fragmentation negatively impacts their TV experience.”

Users are also likely to stop using a streaming service if they struggle to find something they want to watch, per the survey. Forty-nine percent of users said they “are willing to cancel a service based on difficulty finding what to watch.” Additionally, 19 percent of respondents said they would “abandon a viewing session if their content search is not successful.”

Although Tubi users don’t have paid subscriptions to cancel, making it easier to find relevant content could help Tubi grow its user base and increase the time people spend watching, which supports the advertising business Tubi relies on.

Sharable watchlists are rare among streaming services. Mubi has a similar feature where users can make lists of movies and shows that people can follow, but the lists can feature content that’s not available on Mubi.

Plex and JustWatch also let people create and share curated watchlists with other users.

Still, it’s nice to see a streaming service, especially a free one, add new capabilities at a time when many other streaming services are consistently increasing subscription prices. And while some streaming service companies are turning to AI to help with content recommendations, a human connection may appeal more to certain users, while keeping costs lower for Tubi.

#303. iFixit teardown shows how Apple's glowing PROLED MacBook logo works

The new laptop goes the extra mile to recreate the iconic feature.

iFixit has shared its teardown of Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro and besides bemoaning the company's half-hearted commitment to user repairability, it also showed off the physical components that make the laptop's glowing logo work. The new lid design is one of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display's many charms, alongside its tandem OLED display and lighter weight.

Older LCD MacBooks featured a physical cutout that let the display's backlight illuminate the logo, but since OLED screens don't require backlights, Apple had to come up with a different solution to bring the design element back. iFixit found that the company uses a light strip with four LEDs layered behind the display, whose light is reflected through a diffuser to illuminate the logo. The Apple logo itself is also coated "like a two-way mirror," according to iFixit, so that it can appear metallic and reflective when the logo is off, but still let light through when the LEDs are on.

Apple ditched the glowing logo in 2016, so it's a bit ironic that the company waited until it stopped using backlit displays to bring it back. It used to be a cool bit of branding before, but now the company may see the glowing logo design as an important way to distinguish its most expensive laptop from the kind we peons are forced to use.

The rest of the internal changes to the laptop are more expected. Apple was able to achieve the new MacBook Pro's lighter weight by using less aluminum in the base and lid of the laptop and including a slightly smaller trackpad. The laptop's hinge was also reworked to make the display wobble less when you tap the screen. Those changes don't make it any easier to fix, though. The laptop is still complex to disassemble: For example, iFixit says that you have to remove the laptop's logic board to switch out its USB-C ports. Plenty of other components, like the MacBook's memory and the HDMI port, are also soldered in place. Anyone dropping up to $15,000 on a laptop probably isn't worried about doing their own repairs, but Apple's thin and light (and glowing) design comes with some tradeoffs, as always.

Germany is commemorating the Nazi-led November pogroms 88 years ago. Events are also being held to mark the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. DW has more.

These updates are closed. This was a roundup of the stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on Monday, November 9, 2026:

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Monday spoke of the "darkness and light" that Germany experienced on November 9 in remarks made at the sixth annual meeting of the Weimar Forum for Remembrance.

Steinmeier noted that the date had seen the proclamation of the Weimar Republic in 1918 and Germany's first attempt at democracy as well as the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, but that it also marks one of the darkest chapters in German history with the anti-Jewish pogroms of 1938.

Steinmeier used these events to declare Germany's "obligation to observe historical truths, and to remain true to them" calling for the expansion of history lessons that can speak across generations rather than cutting them from school curriculums.

Speaking of the memory of the victims of Nazism, he said Germany should maintain its tradition of installing "Stolpersteine" (stumbling stones) in city sidewalks to mark the sites where Jews had once lived before they were sent to death camps.

The comment comes after a recent decision by the far-right AfD and the conservative CDU to ban the stones in the eastern city of Heidenau.   Monuments to those killed by the Nazis "don't belong on the edge of town, but rather there where victims once lived — in the center of our cities, of our society," Steinmeier said.

He also warned against coopting former concentration camps for political messaging related to conflicts today.

These "memorials are dedicated to the victims of the Nazis, the victims of the Holocaust. They must not become a place to fight over the conflict in the Middle East."

Steinmeier added he was ashamed by today's growing antisemitism.

"We must stand up to hatred of Jews, regardless of whether it originates from the political fringes on the right and left, from the center of society or from Islamism."

#300. Why your Roku might be plugged into the wrong HDMI port

Your Roku might lose a few features if you plug it into any old HDMI port on your TV.

Depending on your smart TV, an add-on media streaming device isn't necessarily essential, but they can still provide a lot of value. Perhaps your TV's processor can't keep up with the latest apps and features, or you might prefer a specific ecosystem. That's what Apple is banking on to sell the 2026 Apple TV 4K, which is now an extremely pricey box at $299.

Roku streamers are far cheaper, but can still come with other concerns. You might be worried about your Roku monitoring what you watch, for example, or the implications of Fox's pending takeover. On a more mundane level, there's an issue applicable to any connected device: getting the best possible performance from your TV.

To do that, it's vital to you select the right HDMI port and cable. It's hard to go too far wrong with Roku devices, but a mistake could still mean getting inferior video or sound.

The reason it's hard to go wrong is that for the most part, Roku devices don't exploit any features unique to HDMI 2.1 or later, and all modern TVs support at least HDMI 2.0. Standards like 4K, HDR10+, Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision can all work over 2.0, if not necessarily in their optimal form. Optimal would include 120Hz-plus refresh rates — but even Roku's top-of-the-line Ultra is capped at 60Hz, regardless of which port you plug it into.

That's acceptable, since 24fps is the most common playback speed for TV and movies while 30fps is used for news. 60fps content (equaling 60Hz) is common on YouTube, Twitch and many live TV streaming services; any modern Roku will support this. 120Hz would simply enable clearer motion, which is mostly relevant for gaming.

The Roku Ultra does support an HDMI 2.1 feature called Quick Media Switching (QMS). This allows refresh rates to shift up or down seamlessly, like if you're flipping from the 30fps evening news to the 24fps cinematic standard. Without QMS, you're going to run into temporary blackouts when a frame rate shift occurs.

In some cases, only certain HDMI ports on your TV will support HDR standards like Dolby Vision. Or if that barrier doesn't exist, you might have to go into your TV's input settings to flip a port over to the appropriate "enhanced" option. Ports are often set to reduced capabilities by default for the sake of compatibility. But since it's unlikely that you'd run into conflicts, you might as well enable modern functionality across the board. Check your manufacturer's website to figure out which ports support HDR and which menus you might need to navigate.

Another important point here is that you shouldn't plug a Roku into your TV's ARC or eARC port. While that technology is essential for some audio features like Dolby Atmos, labeled ports are intended for compatible output devices like soundbars, receivers and other speaker systems. If a TV supports ARC or eARC, it's automatically pulling audio from every HDMI 2.x input, regardless of how it's marked.

Along with the right ports, it's also important to choose a matching cable. If your Roku does support HDMI 2.1 features, a 2.0 cable will prevent them from working. If there's any doubt about what you have, HDMI 2.1 and even 2.2 (also known as Ultra96, which is not in wide use yet) cables are easy to find at low prices.

Computers and game consoles should always get priority for available HDMI 2.1 or 2.2 ports, since they can fully take advantage of high refresh rates and VRR (variable refresh rate). Streamers like Rokus are further back in the line, at least until manufacturers start taking advantage of everything newer TVs are capable of.

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#298. What is the average lifespan of recordable Blu-ray discs?

They can last you quite a while, but there are several factors to consider.

At this point, Blu-ray is a niche format, having mostly been supplanted by downloads, streaming and flash storage. But it's easily the format of choice for cinephiles, owing to higher ceilings on picture and audio quality. And if you want to archive files for a long time, Blu-ray may be more affordable, what with flash memory prices spiraling out of control.

How much can you trust recordable Blu-ray discs (BD-R), though? It's not an academic question if the files you're stashing are irreplaceable. If you make a bad decision, you could potentially lose your only digital copies of home videos, say, or a history of all your artistic projects.

Generally speaking, the news here is positive. BD-R may legitimately be your best option. There can be mitigating factors though, such as manufacturing quality, or simply having something to access the content on several years down the road.

Short of accidents, the main threat to Blu-ray discs is something called disc rot. This is actually an umbrella term for various forms of decay. The reflective layer can gradually become oxidized, for example. Moisture might attract mold, or cause the layers of a disc to separate. Then there's the matter of exposure to UV (ultraviolet) light, though that's more likely to cause labeling to fade than harm your data. You can potentially notice rot before popping in a disc — look for signs like discoloration or spots.

According to Canadian Conservation Institute data, the cheapest BD-R discs will last five to 10 years on average. These should be avoided for any kind of archival project, since an external SSD is liable to last at least that long, and possibly several times as much while storing a lot more data. Remember, even the biggest BD-R discs top out at 128GB.

That said, manufacturing quality can have a huge impact. In better BD-Rs, a dye recording layer is replaced by a silicon and copper alloy, which you can tell if a disc appears dark gray or grayish-brown. Likewise, these discs might switch to a gold metal layer. The result, the CCI says, is double the lifespan at 10 to 20 years.

It gets better. BD-RE (rewritable) discs can conceivably last you as much as 20 to 50 years. That's so long that you might be able to pass them down to your children or grandchildren. On those timescales, however, other factors should probably discourage you from relying on Blu-ray.

The most obvious reason is that discs are fragile. While storage in a relatively dry, dark and cool environment can deter rot, it's all too easy to accidentally crack or scratch a disc in a way that leaves it unreadable. Conversely, many external SSDs use tough metal enclosures that make physical destruction unlikely. All it might take to ruin your disc collection is forgetting that it's at the bottom of a moving box you're hauling, not the top.

Ultimately, the bigger issue might be industry support for Blu-ray. Optical drives have vanished as a default feature on computers, and companies are slowly pulling out the market for both external burners and BD-R discs, even Sony. At the moment, it's not that difficult to find burners and discs if you shop online. But there's no telling whether anyone will still be making this hardware 10 years down the road, much less 20. You could end up with an immaculately-preserved collection and no way of accessing it. Even your current drive might become useless if its software drivers cease to be compatible with later operating systems.

Whatever route you take, it's best not to be completely reliant on one storage medium for critical files. The general rule of thumb these days is to keep one copy in the cloud, and two others on separate forms of local storage. That's not always realistic — at the least, however, you should always be in a position to migrate your files to something fresher.

#297. Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?

She would be the first female president and the first Christian Social Union politician to hold Germany's highest office. Ilse Aigner is the favored candidate for the Federal Convention vote on January 30.

Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner has emerged as the leading candidate to succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as president of Germany, a largely ceremonial office, but who is the head of state and regarded as a moral authority for the nation.

News emerged over the weekend that Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader Friedrich Merz favored Aigner, a veteran of the CDU's sister-party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and currently president of the Bavarian parliament.

A specially convened assembly, the Federal Convention, will gather on January 30, 2027, to elect the next German president. Since the CDU, CSU, and their coalition partner the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have a majority in the convention, Aigner's election is considered highly likely.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Aigner is in many respects an unusual politician, especially in Germany, where a law degree often seems to be a prerequisite for a political career. The 61-year-old has no university degree at all, though she did train as a telecommunications technician to join her parents' electrical business.

She spent several years working for the military helicopter company Eurocopter, since bought by the aviation and defense giant Airbus, where she developed electrical components.

Aigner entered the Bavarian parliament for the CSU in 1994 and then served from 1998 to 2013 in Germany's federal parliament, the Bundestag. From 2008 to 2013, she was agriculture and consumer protection minister under then Chancellor Angela Merkel.

Both of these portfolios come with considerable pressure from the public, especially during food scandals, and from powerful lobbying organizations, as well as conflicts at EU level. Aigner navigated this period without any major crises and was generally well regarded.

The personnel policies of political parties can often seem like a game of chess. In 2013, Aigner left national politics and moved back to her home state to serve as Bavaria's economy minister under then State Premier Horst Seehofer, who tried to establish her as his successor.

But then came Markus Söder, at the time Bavaria's finance minister and for a long time Seehofer's biggest rival inside the CSU. It was Söder, a colorful character who also harbored pretensions to be German chancellor, who won out in the power struggle that followed Seehofer's retirement and became Bavarian state premier in 2018.

Aigner and Söder both entered Bavaria's state parliament in 1994, when they were the state's two youngest lawmakers, and their political paths have been intertwined since. Though Söder's rise to power prevented Aigner from becoming state premier, she has served as president of Bavaria's state parliament for the past eight years, and is a highly respected authority figure in the state.

For months now, Aigner has been named as a potential candidate for Germany's head of state after Steinmeier's constitutionally enforced exit next year.

Söder himself openly mentioned her as a suitable candidate back in April, and there have been indications of support from several CDU and CSU representatives, but also from the ranks of the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But Merz seemed wary for a long time. Other names came — and went.

When the chancellor greeted Aigner by name in his opening remarks to a CSU meeting in Munich in October, he had to pause for thunderous applause from the delegates, who rose to their feet to celebrate the veteran politician.

In January, the Bavarian Merkur newspaper reported on Aigner's visit to a school in the town of Tegernsee, where she answered questions from fourth graders for their student newspaper. The CSU politician told them that she had not planned her career, but she was never able to "keep her mouth shut" and this was also part of why she had been elected to her various offices.

However, it was also noticeable that she was entirely capable of "keeping her mouth shut" when it was judicious to do so: She has largely refrained from commenting publicly during the internal maneuvering for the candidacy within the Union parties.

Aigner would not only be Germany's first female president, but also the first to be single and never married. Though men have dominated the office, there have been female nominees in almost every election since 1999. That year, the Union put forward Thuringian physicist Dagmar Schipanski, while the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), precursor to the socialist Left Party, put forward theologian Uta Ranke-Heinemann in the race against Social Democrat Johannes Rau.

But considering the majority needed in the Federal Convention, both were effectively just token candidates from minority parties, as have been all the other female candidates since. That's one reason why there has been pressure to finally choose a woman as the majority candidate. Aigner has long enjoyed respect from the conservative camp.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany has never had a president, or indeed a chancellor, from the CSU, a regional party that nevertheless wields national power thanks to its alliance with the CDU. One CSU lawmaker, Richard Stücklen, spent four years as president of the Bundestag — formally the country's second-highest office — from 1979.

If the door to the presidency does open for Aigner, many believe it would shut out Söder's ambitions to become chancellor. The CDU, a much bigger conservative party, usually overrules the CSU when it comes to choosing a chancellor candidate when the general election comes around, and it seems unlikely that the CDU would tolerate two CSU figures leading the country.

But Aigner's election would also remove one of Söder's key rivals back home: Aigner, still only 61, enjoys excellent popularity ratings and is considered a natural rival to the 59-year-old state premier.

Ultimately, by nominating Aigner, Merz is also paving the way for someone from the CDU to become the next chancellor provided the CDU/CSU wins the next federal election, of course.

But first, the Federal Convention must make its decision on January 30. The new German president will officially assume office in mid-March.

This article was originally written in German.

Google’s Pixel phones get an update every month, but most are just security patches and bug fixes. The bigger changes are bundled into quarterly Pixel Drops, and one is rolling out today. The update brings a few new things, and many of the Gemini features previously exclusive to the latest Pixel phones will also expand to Google’s Pixel 10 lineup.

The Pixel 11 was Google’s first foray into “Gemini Intelligence” branding, something we’ll see a lot more of going forward. Some of the features under that heading were limited to Google’s newest phones (and in some cases, Samsung’s phones). The November Pixel Drop will expand these AI features to the Pixel 10 lineup, but importantly, that doesn’t include the budget-oriented Pixel 10a.

For starters, the Pixel 10 series will get the improved personalized suggestions (previously known as Magic Cue) that debuted on the Pixel 11. This enables things like sending grocery lists to Google Keep from other apps and generating summaries from the context menu. This feature is still limited to select apps in rideshare, food delivery, travel, and a few other categories.

The AI-powered icon theming that Google added to Pixels back in March is also getting an update. Initially, this feature just matched icon colors to the system theme when developers didn’t include the necessary theming assets. With this update, Google says it has moved the feature to a more powerful Nano Banana model, unlocking 10 new icon styles for your home screen.

The update also brings Create My Widget to Pixel phones. Google announced this earlier in 2026, and it shipped on Googlebooks a few weeks ago. The idea is that you describe a home screen widget you want, and Android builds it for you on the spot. However, the use cases are pretty narrow. You’re limited to data accessible in search (e.g., stock prices, sports scores, and weather) and select Google account data points like Gmail or your calendar.

So that’s a lot of AI. Google does have some non-AI additions with this update, but don’t get your hopes up. One of the headlining additions is (drumroll) HiLight support for Google Messages. Yes, Pixel 11 phones will be able to illuminate HiLight when you get a message from important contacts. Ignoring that we had more functional notification LEDs 20 years ago, this is a good and necessary improvement for Google’s least useful hardware feature.

The wearable can also log reps and weights as you go without interrupting live metrics. While Create My Widget is not yet available on the watch, Google promises it’s also coming soon.

The update is beginning its rollout today and should be available widely in the coming days.

#294. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

#293. Google Fi adds support for a second 5G network, won't say which one

Fi has always supported T-Mobile, but the new one? Google won’t say.

Google has announced a “super network” upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it’s adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one.

Google’s MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google’s Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel.

With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. Google’s blog post announcing the change conspicuously doesn’t mention either network, saying only that it supports “two of America’s best 5G cellular networks.”

We know one of them is T-Mobile, and the other must be either AT&T or Verizon. When reached for comment, a Google spokesperson declined to name the second network, which is odd. Looking at the Fi coverage map, my best guess for the super network partner is Verizon. The shape of unserved regions is a closer match than AT&T, but carriers do tend to fudge the fine details of these maps.

MVNOs don’t always advertise which network they use, and that information is getting harder to find in FAQs and support pages. Google’s Fi FAQ no longer even confirms T-Mobile as a network partner. Google used to be very upfront about its partnership with T-Mobile, pointing out that, unlike most MVNOs, it gets top prioritization on T-Mobile’s towers. Network information like this is really something consumers should have when shopping for plans—you probably know which carriers work best where you spend your time.

There are a few caveats in the super network rollout beyond the mysterious new partner. Currently, network switching is only supported on the Pixel 9, Pixel 10, and Pixel 11 series. Other devices will get access in 2027. You also won’t be able to enjoy traditional dual-SIM functionality if you want Fi to switch networks. This will only work if you have Fi configured as an eSIM with all non-Fi SIMs disabled.

If you meet those requirements, super network support is rolling out now at no additional cost on Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

#292. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#291. Lucid CEO says the company didn't know where its own cars were

Gaps in its logistics system caused the EV maker to lose orders.

Lucid, the California-based Tesla rival that makes luxury EVs like the Air and Gravity, has an interesting excuse for its third quarter earnings underperformance. The company said it lost sales due to inventory control issues, with CEO Silvio Napoli admitting in an earnings call that sometimes "we did not even know where cars were." That chaos resulted in slow delivery times up to two weeks that caused Lucid to lose orders from impatient buyers.

The company doesn't have millions of cars to keep track of like Tesla, either. Lucid built just 2,954 vehicles last quarter and delivered 3,806, down seven percent from the year before. Building fewer cars than it sold helped it reduce inventory, but it still had $1.22 billion worth on the books at the end of September.

With its logistics issues, Lucid's sales suffered like Tesla's did when the latter started ramping up the Model 3. Elon Musk's company had to take drastic measures to solve supply issues (like building its own car carriers and buying trucking companies), but once it did, sales took off.

Lucid's Napoli suggested that its latest fixes to shipping problems will have a similar effect by allowing the commercial team to "sell the cars that we know can be available on the day for the customers who require it." With that, along with a growing US EV market due to high gas prices (plus a deal it recently cut with robotaxi company Bolt), the company has positive expectations for the latter half of 2026.

Fixing its supply chain won't solve Lucid's other problems, though, like quality control issues and customer service complaints. The other tiny issue is that the automaker lost $831 million last quarter on revenue of just $350 million, due to cost of making each vehicle that far exceeds the selling price. However, that didn't discourage the company's primary investor, the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF), from injecting an additional $1.75 billion into Lucid.

#289. EU aims to pick new ECB chief by year-end

Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.

The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, announced on October 29 that she is stepping down from the position prematurely, nine months ⁠before ⁠the end of her term.

Lagarde's decision to step down early makes the schedule tight for EU leaders because they must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board ​within months.

"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in ​the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.

The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International ​Settlements, Pablo ‌Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.

The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.

Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position," referring to his long-standing experience.

"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfill this position."

Heinen also ​said countries should ‌not see the ECB leadership contest as ​one between northern ⁠and southern European countries, or as ⁠an "​opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel ‌Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, ​whose term ends ⁠in May 2027.

The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the ⁠main eurozone countries — ​France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.

The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.

"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.

Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.

"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

#288. Apple is shutting down its online Support Community on November 20

It’ll remain online, but it will no longer accept new posts.

If you ever want to ask fellow Apple users anything about the company's devices in the future, you'll have to go on social media websites. The company is permanently shutting down the official Apple Support Community. As MacRumors has noticed, Apple posted a message on the community home page, which says that it's closing down on November 20. While the support website is still up, you can no longer post in it, and it's only available in a read-only state.

The community has gone through several changes over the years since it debuted in 1998. It was known as Apple Discussions for a time, before it was renamed to its current one. User responses on the Support Community are typically some of the first results to pop up whenever you search for technical issues you need an answer to or for instructions on how to use a particular feature. Some of those responses are helpful, but some are admittedly not. In its announcement, Apple says "you can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site."

In a statement, Apple told MacRumors that it decided to shut down down the Support Community "after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs." Maybe the community has just outlived its usefulness. Since people have other places online they can go to when seeking advice from other users anyway, Apple may have decided it was time to let the discussions forum go.
